design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial in an inpatient research unit: 20 adults with cocaine dependence, recruited by newspaper advertisement and admitted soon after last use, were randomized 1:1 to modafinil or placebo for the first weeks of abstinence. Nocturnal polysomnography on three nights in each of abstinence weeks 1, 2 and 3 (averaged per week), multiple sleep latency tests on one day each week, morning and evening visual analogue sleep and alertness ratings and the Stanford Sleepiness Scale. Twelve healthy men without drug use, recorded on a single night after an adaptation night, served as an unrandomized reference group for week 3.
can_establish: Whether modafinil, compared with placebo, changed polysomnographic sleep, daytime sleep latency and self-rated sleep and sleepiness during the first three weeks of supervised abstinence; and, as an observational time trend within both arms, how measured and self-rated sleep changed over those weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether modafinil helps sleep outside a supervised inpatient unit with fixed bedtimes, no caffeine and no napping, or whether better sleep reduces relapse (not tested); whether the sleep changes over abstinence are caused by stopping cocaine rather than by the unit routine (no group that kept using, and no group without cocaine dependence followed over the same weeks); effects in people who use cocaine without dependence.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper advertisements for cocaine research: 44 passed phone screening, 29 qualified at interview, 21 entered and 20 completed; most saw the study as their only route to inpatient treatment (Methods › Cocaine Dependent Participants; Patient perspectives).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV current cocaine dependence by psychiatrist interview; urine positive for cocaine and negative for other drugs at admission. Excluded: chronic medical or neurological conditions, dependence on substances other than cocaine and nicotine, other Axis I diagnoses, psychoactive prescription medicines in the past year; no history of a sleep disorder, and light caffeine use only.
sample.demographics: Mean age 44 (SD 7) with placebo and 40 (SD 5) with modafinil; 16 men and 4 women (9 and 1 with placebo, 7 and 3 with modafinil); 13 African American and 7 white; 3.2 and 3.3 days since last cocaine use on the first study day; baseline Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index 4.3 and 3.5; self-reported use in the previous 90 days given in Table 1 (some cells garbled; see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: One of 21 left voluntarily shortly after admission and was not analysed (arm not stated); all 20 others completed.
sample.selection_effects: Mostly treatment-seeking volunteers (18 of 20 in the text, 16 of 20 in Table 1) without other psychiatric or sleep disorders, light caffeine use and limited other substance use; paid $500 for completion.

exposure.measurement: Randomized, double-blind study medicine given on the unit; abstinence confirmed by urine screens three times a week in a supervised unit.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: modafinil 400 mg or placebo by mouth every morning at 07:30 for 16 days (study days 1 to 16), starting within 3 days of admission, that is between the 2nd and 6th day of abstinence; the dose could be lowered to 200 mg for intolerance and was lowered in one participant on days 3 and 4 because of palpitations. Fixed time in bed 23:00 to 07:00; polysomnography on nights 1 to 3, 7 to 9 and 14 to 16 after an adaptation night; multiple sleep latency tests at 11:30, 14:00 and 16:30 on days 2, 8 and 15 (three naps, ended after three epochs of sleep); Stanford Sleepiness Scale at 10:00, 15:30 and 21:00. Caffeine-free unit, no daytime napping, smoking allowed at three 15-minute outdoor breaks a day.
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other substances (except nicotine) excluded; urine negative for other drugs at admission. Past-90-day alcohol use averaged 117 (SD 133) drinks with placebo and 75 (SD 86) with modafinil; no participant showed alcohol withdrawal. Tobacco smoking continued at set breaks.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Supervised inpatient abstinence verified by urine toxicology three times a week; study weeks 1 to 3 correspond roughly to abstinence days 2 to 6 through about day 20.

comparison.controls: Placebo arm (10). For the week-3 comparison, 12 healthy men aged 30 to 50 (mean 39, SD 9) with no drug or psychiatric history, sleeping in the same laboratory for one adaptation and one experimental night but living outside the unit and receiving no capsule.
comparison.matching: Randomization 1:1 (method and concealment not described); the arms did not differ significantly in age, sex, race, substance use, days abstinent or baseline sleep quality (Table 1). The healthy men were chosen to match the age range; they drank less alcohol and had non-significantly lower baseline PSQI.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep before cocaine use is unknown; the healthy reference group differs in sex, setting, number of recorded nights and drug history.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Healthy reference men had no substance use history, including nicotine.

outcomes.instruments: Polysomnography (two central EEG channels, EOG, chin EMG, ECG; scored to American Academy of Sleep Medicine criteria by one scorer blinded to study day and group): sleep onset latency, total sleep time, N1-2, N3 (slow-wave) and REM time, REM latency. Modified multiple sleep latency test. Visual analogue ratings on waking (sleep quality, depth, feeling rested, alertness) and at bedtime (alertness that day). Stanford Sleepiness Scale three times a day. Adverse events.
outcomes.validity_norms: Polysomnography and the multiple sleep latency test are standard, though the test was shortened here and occipital leads were missing; the visual analogue scales are based on the St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire.
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep disturbance as longer sleep latency, shorter total sleep and less slow-wave or REM sleep; 'normalizing' as no significant difference from the healthy reference group at week 3.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six polysomnographic measures, daytime sleep latency, five visual analogue ratings and the Stanford Sleepiness Scale were each tested for drug, week and interaction effects, with post-hoc tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Polysomnograms scored blind to day and group; blinding of the sleep latency tests not stated; self-ratings by participants (blinding integrity not assessed).

analysis.effect_sizes: Linear mixed models (treatment between, week within). Modafinil main effects: sleep onset latency F(1,18) = 5.8, p = 0.027; N3 time F(1,18) = 11.9, p = 0.0029. Drug by week interactions: total sleep time F(2,36) = 7.4, p = 0.0021; REM latency F(2,36) = 3.6, p = 0.039; REM time F(2,36) = 3.5, p = 0.04; week-3 post hoc: longer total sleep F(1,36) = 6.7, p = 0.013, shorter REM latency F(1,36) = 6.9, p = 0.013, REM time not different at any week (p > 0.17). Daytime sleep latency, week 1: 15 (SEM 2) minutes with modafinil against 10 (SEM 2) with placebo, F(1,36) = 4.4, p = 0.04. Stanford Sleepiness Scale: drug trend F(1,144) = 3.4, p = 0.069; drug by week by time-of-day interaction F(4,144) = 2.7, p = 0.036. Group means for the polysomnographic measures are shown only in figures, so no standardized effect sizes or intervals can be given.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration is mentioned (page searched for registration terms).
analysis.selective_reporting: All planned sleep outcomes appear to be reported, but only as test statistics and figures; no means, SDs or intervals for the polysomnographic outcomes are given in the text.
analysis.power: The authors say the study was powered only to detect the previously observed changes over abstinence within each group, not drug effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over three weeks of supervised abstinence, measured sleep got worse on most measures (longer time to fall asleep, shorter total and REM sleep) while slow-wave sleep rose and self-rated sleep improved. Compared with placebo, modafinil shortened time to fall asleep and increased slow-wave sleep throughout, lengthened total sleep and shortened REM latency in week 3, lengthened daytime sleep latency in week 1 only, and lowered some daytime sleepiness ratings; it did not change self-rated sleep. More people on modafinil had adverse events (6 of 10 against 2 of 10).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that modafinil "promotes nocturnal sleep, normalizes sleep architecture, and decreases daytime sleepiness". Gaps: (1) 'normalizes' rests on post-hoc comparisons at one week with 12 unrandomized healthy men recorded on one night outside the unit, and total sleep with modafinil was still below theirs; (2) the abstract says abstinence worsened all measured outcomes, but slow-wave sleep increased; (3) the discussion says modafinil reduced the REM-sleep deficit, but no week showed a REM-time difference; (4) the daytime-sleepiness benefit on the objective test was confined to week 1; (5) adverse events, more frequent with modafinil, are not weighed in the conclusions. The authors acknowledge the small sample and powering.

timeline.event: Morgan et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend 82:238-249) describe 'occult insomnia': measured sleep worsening over abstinence while self-rated sleep improves, in a separate inpatient sample from the same group.
This trial: first study of modafinil on sleep in people abstinent from cocaine, by the authors' account; it reproduces the 2006 time course in its placebo arm.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small trial of modafinil on sleep; the abstinence time course has been reported by the same group in earlier samples (not read here), so it is replicated only within one team. Larger outpatient trials of modafinil for cocaine dependence exist but were not read for this card.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants DA011744-06 and KL2RR024138; State of Connecticut Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Yale University and Harvard Medical School sleep researchers; the first author also reported palpitations with modafinil in a letter cited in the paper.

what_would_settle_it: A larger, registered, double-blind trial of modafinil against placebo (and against non-drug sleep support) in people stopping cocaine, with outpatient sleep measured objectively, a healthy and a continuing-use comparison followed over the same weeks, blinding checked, adverse events recorded, and relapse as an outcome.

domains.note: Randomized 1:1; sequence generation and concealment not described; arms similar at baseline on the tabulated variables.
Double-blind with placebo, but modafinil is a wake-promoting drug and adverse events were three times as frequent on it; blinding integrity not checked. Inpatient routine identical across arms.
One of 21 left shortly after admission; all 20 others completed.
Polysomnography scored blind to day and group (low risk); self-rated sleep and sleepiness by participants who may have recognised modafinil.
No registration; 13 outcomes each tested for several effects without correction; values reported mostly as test statistics and figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Some concerns rather than high because the main sleep outcomes are objective and blind-scored and attrition is negligible; the concerns are the undescribed randomization, possible functional unblinding for self-ratings, many outcomes without correction and no registration. With 10 people per arm, the estimates are imprecise. May be cited for the direction of modafinil's effects on polysomnographic sleep and sleepiness under inpatient conditions, and, as an observational time trend, for measured sleep worsening while self-rated sleep improves over early cocaine abstinence; not for 'normal' sleep with modafinil, nor for effects outside a supervised unit.

key_findings.finding: Of 44 people with cocaine problems who passed phone screening, 29 qualified, 21 entered and 20 completed (10 modafinil, 10 placebo); the arms were similar in age (44 and 40), sex, race, days since last cocaine use (3.2 and 3.3), substance use and baseline sleep quality.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Cocaine Dependent Participants; Results › Demographics; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Across both arms, abstinence week affected every polysomnographic measure; from week 1 to week 3 sleep onset latency increased (t(36) = -4.9, p < 0.0001), total sleep time fell (t(36) = 2.8, p = 0.008), REM sleep time fell (t(36) = 3.0, p = 0.005), REM latency increased (t(36) = -4.0, p = 0.0003) and slow-wave (N3) sleep time increased (t(36) = -3.5, p = 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Over the same weeks, participants rated their sleep and alertness as improving: main effects of week on overall sleep quality (F(2,36) = 9.0, p = 0.0007), depth of sleep (6.3, p = 0.0044), feeling rested (5.9, p = 0.0063), alertness on waking (8.3, p = 0.0011) and daytime alertness (7.2, p = 0.0023); modafinil had no effect on any of these ratings (all p > 0.35).
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Modafinil against placebo: shorter sleep onset latency (F(1,18) = 5.8, p = 0.027) and more slow-wave sleep (F(1,18) = 11.9, p = 0.0029; more than double the placebo value at all time points, per the Discussion) across weeks; in week 3, longer total sleep time (F(1,36) = 6.7, p = 0.013) and shorter REM latency (F(1,36) = 6.9, p = 0.013); REM sleep time did not differ at any week (all p > 0.17).
key_findings.locator: Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Daytime sleep latency on the multiple sleep latency test: no main effect of modafinil or week; modafinil gave a longer latency only in week 1 (15, SEM 2, against 10, SEM 2, minutes; F(1,36) = 4.4, p = 0.04).

Stanford Sleepiness Scale: a trend for less sleepiness with modafinil (F(1,144) = 3.4, p = 0.069) and a drug by week by time-of-day interaction (F(4,144) = 2.7, p = 0.036); post hoc, modafinil went with less sleepiness at the morning ratings and at the afternoon ratings in weeks 2 and 3, and no change at the evening rating.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: At week 3, against 12 healthy men: significant three-group differences in slow-wave sleep (F(2,29) = 4.9, p = 0.015), REM time (3.5, p = 0.04), total sleep time (12.1, p < 0.0001), sleep onset latency (4.7, p = 0.017), N1-2 time and REM latency; post hoc, slow-wave sleep with modafinil did not differ from the healthy men, REM time was lower and sleep latency longer with placebo (not with modafinil) than in the healthy men, and total sleep with modafinil remained non-significantly below theirs. Self-rated sleep quality did not differ (placebo 77, SE 5; modafinil 81, SE 5; healthy 67, SE 6; p = 0.16).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparisons to Controls; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: 8 participants (6 on modafinil, 2 on placebo) had 9 events; headache in 4 on modafinil and 1 on placebo, nausea without vomiting in 2 on modafinil, palpitations in 1 on modafinil (seen in the emergency department; dose temporarily reduced), conjunctivitis in 1 on placebo; the others were mild.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says progressive abstinence worsened all measured polysomnographic outcomes, but slow-wave (N3) sleep time increased from week 1 to week 3 (t(36) = -3.5, p = 0.001), as the Discussion acknowledges.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence course is not uniformly worse; slow-wave sleep rose while other measures worsened.

reporting_issues.issue: The P values for the effect of abstinence week on REM sleep time (F(2,36) = 8.4, printed p = 0.0002) and REM latency (F(2,36) = 11.1, printed p = 0.001) appear swapped: the editors' calculation gives p of about 0.001 and 0.0002 respectively.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Both effects remain significant; the printed values should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 18 of the 20 participants were seeking treatment; Table 1 gives 8 of 10 in each arm (16 of 20).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Inpatient Facility; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sample was mostly treatment-seeking either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 renders some cells with stray spaces (44 2 then 9; 31 1 then 6; 50 3 then 9), so the past-90-day cocaine days and grams cannot be read directly; read as 44 (SD 29) against 31 (SD 16) days and 50 (SD 39) against 40 (SD 25) grams they reproduce the printed P values of 0.25 and 0.47 approximately (editors' check: about 0.23 and 0.50).
reporting_issues.consequence: Baseline cocaine use should be quoted from the published version, not from this rendering.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says modafinil reduced the development of REM sleep deficits over abstinence, but post-hoc tests found no difference in REM sleep time between arms at any week (all p > 0.17).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, final paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The claimed REM benefit rests on an interaction without a difference at any time point.

reporting_issues.issue: Polysomnographic means and SDs are given only in figures (images); the text reports test statistics only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of modafinil's effects (for example, minutes of extra sleep) cannot be stated from the text.
